# Jacek Karpiński — Summary
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer born in Turin, Italy, into a distinguished family of alpinists and intellectuals. Overcoming wartime injuries as a teenage resistance fighter in World War II, he excelled academically and entered the field of electrical engineering. After initial setbacks due to political distrust of his Home Army background, he joined the Polish Academy of Sciences, contributing to the development of early computing devices.
Karpiński's major achievements include constructing the AAH for meteorology, the groundbreaking AKAT-1—the world’s first transistor-based differential equations analyzer—and the perceptron, an early object recognition device. He designed Poland’s fastest computer of its time, KAR-65. His most renowned project was the K-202 minicomputer in the 1970s, noted for its advanced architecture and innovations, but its mass production was thwarted due to a mix of political, economic, and institutional opposition. Later in life, he worked abroad and attempted business ventures, though with limited success, and earned high national honors for his engineering contributions. Karpiński's legacy also includes controversy over his role as an informant for Polish intelligence, mainly reporting on scientific progress, and ongoing debates about the true impact of his technical innovations.
